paper.title: The Importance of Peer Quality for Completion of Higher Education
paper.code_data_availability: No data or code availability statement and no Statistics Denmark project reference appear in the paper. …

registers.name_in_paper: several administrative registers (Danish administrative data; no register is named individually)
registers.role: sample frame, treatment, outcomes and controls
variables_mentioned: high school GPA (standardized within year of high school graduation)
high school course-specific grades in mathematics and Danish (from 1998)
high school type (STX, HF, HTX, HHX) and year of high school graduation
education program and institution of enrollment, and year of enrollment
dropout from / completion of the enrolled education program

linkages: Students linked to their peers through education-by-institution cells in the year of enrollment (for programs with two intakes per year, peer groups are separated by September/February intake)
Students linked to their parents for parental education and parental income

Students linked to their high school graduation cohort, to standardize HS GPA within year of graduation and to identify 'old peers' from the student's own high school who also enter the higher-education peer group
Enrollments linked over time to the same individual, so repeat enrollments are observed (the sample is not restricted to first-time enrollments)
Enrollments linked to later labor market records to construct average employment and earnings 7-12 years after enrollment

sample.universe: The universe of higher education enrollments -- university and professional bachelor programs -- in Denmark in the period 1985-2010; 1,203,232 enrollments across 822,664 individuals before exclusions
sample.unit_of_observation: enrollment (individual x education x institution x year of enrollment)
selection_rules: Start from all 1,203,232 enrollments in higher education observed in Denmark 1985-2010 (822,664 individuals); the sample is not restricted to first-time enrollments
Delete 9,654 observations where the peer group consists of three students or less
Exclude 2,847 observations where there is no observable value of peer group ability
Exclude 4,025 enrollments where there is only one observable high school GPA for the peer group
Drop 2,616 enrollments in an education-by-institution combination that only exists for one particular cohort
Resulting estimation sample: 1,184,090 enrollments (813,337 individuals) across 1,181 education-by-institution combinations
sample.period: 1985-2010 (enrollment years); 1985-2006 for the labor market outcome regressions

construction_notes: High school GPAs are standardized within year of high school graduation to account for grade inflation

Peers' HS GPA is the leave-one-out average of the standardized GPA within the education-by-institution entry cohort; for students without an observable own HS GPA the peer group average of observable values is imputed instead of the leave-one-out average

29% of students in the sample have no (observable) high school degree recorded; HS GPA is available for STX and HF graduates from 1978 and for HTX and HHX graduates from 1999; own HS GPA is set to zero if missing and a missing-HS-GPA dummy is included

Ability deciles and the low/middle/high ability groups are defined from the distribution of HS GPA in the student's year of high school graduation (absolute ranking, Table 13) or within the education-by-institution unit (relative ranking, Table 14)
Low-GPA = below the 20th percentile, high-GPA = above the 80th percentile, middle-GPA = 20th to 80th percentile; shares of high- and low-GPA peers omit own value
Peer characteristics are peer group averages of the individual characteristics, omitting own value
The ability measure of 'old peers' -- peers from the student's own high school graduation cohort who also enter the higher-education peer group -- is added as a control
An education-by-institution unit is defined as selective if the cohort-average HS GPA of enrollments is in the top 20th percentile for more than 50% of the years the program is offered
Parents' income and labor market earnings are deflated using the Danish CPI to 2015 prices; parents' income is measured in 100,000 DKK and labor market earnings in 1,000 DKK
Labor market outcomes are averages over the period 7-12 years after enrollment
Education programs are grouped into four fields -- STEM, Social Science, Arts, Health -- per Table A1
Standard errors are clustered at the education-by-institution level throughout

links.pointer_quote: Overall, we find that a one standard deviation increase in peers' high school GPA reduces the probability of dropping out by 4.6 percentage points.

claims.statement: Among all enrollments in higher education in Denmark 1985-2010 in the estimation sample (university and professional bachelor programs), a one standard deviation increase in peers' average standardized high school GPA reduces the probability of dropping out of the higher education program the student enrolled in.

definition.value: Leave-one-out average of the standardized high school GPA of the student's peer group, where the peer group is all students enrolling in the same education program at the same institution in the same year; high school GPA is standardized within year of high school graduation. For students without an observable own HS GPA the measure is the peer group average of observable values rather than the leave-one-out average.

timing.value: Predetermined: high school GPA is determined before enrollment in higher education; the peer measure is fixed at the year of enrollment in the education-by-institution cell.

definition.value: Indicator that the student eventually drops out of (rather than completes) the higher education program they enrolled in; students are followed over time until dropout or completion is observed.

timing.value: Measured over the full follow-up of the enrollment spell; the paper states no fixed horizon for the baseline dropout measure.

units.value: change in the probability of dropping out (0-1 scale) per one standard deviation increase in peers' average standardized high school GPA

magnitude.interpretation: We find that dropout decreases by 4.6 percentage points when peers' GPA increases by a standard deviation.

identification.source_of_variation: Idiosyncratic cohort-to-cohort variation in the average high school GPA of entering students within education-by-institution cells, 1985-2010, arising from institutions' discretion over quota 1 versus quota 2 admissions, year-to-year variation in demand for specific programs under the deferred-acceptance Coordinated Enrollment System, and regulation of the supply of study slots

key_assumptions.assumption: The variation in peer composition is exogenous after controlling for education-by-institution fixed effects (plus year fixed effects, education-by-institution linear time trends and the listed individual and peer controls): changes in the peer ability measure within an education-by-institution are uncorrelated with unobserved factors that affect the student's achievement.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Within-between variance decomposition showing that fixed effects and trends remove the between variation while a non-negligible within variation remains (Table 3); balancing tests of the peer ability measure against student and cohort characteristics (Table 4); falsification tests on adjacent cohorts (Appendix Table A9)

key_assumptions.assumption: Reflection bias is avoided because the measure of peer ability is predetermined: high school grades are determined before enrollment in higher education, so the student's own dropout decision and peers' behaviour in higher education cannot feed back into the measured peer ability.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Use of high school GPA, fixed before enrollment, following Lavy, Silva and Weinhardt (2012)

key_assumptions.assumption: No education-by-institution specific unobserved time-varying factor drives both the peer composition and the dropout decision beyond what the included education-by-institution linear time trends absorb; the authors concede they cannot rule out systematic correlation with unobservables, in particular in the college sample.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Inclusion of education-by-institution linear time trends; falsification tests in which the spillover effects of adjacent cohorts' ability diminish as the cohort gap expands (Appendix Table A9); Altonji, Elder and Taber (2005) argument that selection on observables indicates selection on unobservables

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on peer-group characteristics: peer groups of three students or fewer, enrollments without an observable peer group ability value, enrollments with only one observable high school GPA in the peer group, and education-by-institution combinations existing for a single cohort are excluded.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The exclusions and their sizes are listed in Section 4.3

implies_edges.from: Sample inclusion: peer group of at least four students with observable peer ability

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across cohorts: the relevant peer group for a student is the own education-by-institution entry cohort, so the ability of adjacent cohorts does not affect own dropout. The paper's own falsification test rejects this for the nearest cohorts -- the ability of peers does have spillover effects on adjacent cohorts -- but finds the effects diminishing as the cohort gap widens.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix Table A9: significant coefficients on the ability of cohorts t-1, t+1 and t+2 whose size and significance diminish as the gap increases

implies_edges.from: Average HS GPA of adjacent (lead and lag) cohorts in the same education-by-institution

key_assumptions.assumption: The peer group is correctly delimited by the education-by-institution entry cohort (split by September/February intake where relevant); the authors acknowledge that in the largest cohorts (up to 1,924 students) not all members are influential peers and that smaller study groups or classrooms are unobserved.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussion in Section 4.1 and robustness to excluding cohorts and programs with more than 500 or 300 students (Table 15)

key_assumptions.assumption: The reduced-form coefficient is not decomposed: it may reflect both contextual peer effects (the effect of peer characteristics) and endogenous peer effects (the effect of peer behaviour) in the sense of Manski (1993), and the paper makes no attempt to separate them.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 5; separation would require additional assumptions and exogenous variation in both contextual and endogenous peer characteristics (Bramoulle, Djebbari and Fortin, 2009)

ambiguities: Polarity of the outcome: 'Dropout' is recorded as higher_is_less because the concept the variable measures is completion of / persistence in higher education, which the paper's title and framing make explicit ('The Importance of Peer Quality for Completion of Higher Education'). A reader who treats 'dropout' itself as the concept would record higher_is_more.

Extraction scope: this file carries one claim per coefficient for the paper's designated parameter of interest (the peer-ability measures) in Table 5 (all five build-up columns), Tables 6-12 (all columns), Table 13 (all of column 1 plus the STEM and Social Science coefficients the text discusses), Table 14 (column 1) and the two course-specific peer-skill coefficients the paper discusses from Table A5. The coefficients on own HS GPA (a control the paper does not designate as a parameter of interest), the remaining field columns of Tables 13-14 and Appendix Tables A2, A6, A7, A8 and A9 are not split into separate claims; they are recorded under identification.robustness_checks and falsification instead.

evidence.how: The table prints no p-values; the coefficient carries '***' and the table note reads '*p < 0.1,**p < 0.05,***p < 0.01', so the printed significance marking means p < 0.01.

The paper never names the estimator. It prints a linear additive estimating equation, reports R-squared and standard errors clustered at the education-by-institution level, and the outcome is a 0/1 indicator, so the estimator is OLS (a linear probability model where the outcome is binary).
Equation (1) transcribed from the printed equation on page 6; subscripts and Greek letters are rendered in ASCII because the published typesetting is lost in the PDF text layer.

prior_findings_compared.as_stated: The size of the effect is very close to the one estimated by Booij et al. (2017). They find that a standard deviation increase in peers' GPA reduces dropout by 4.2 percentage points.

prior_findings_compared.citation: previous studies of peer effects in higher education
prior_findings_compared.as_stated: Hence, our linear-in-means estimate of peer effects has the same order of magnitude as estimates found in previous studies.

ambiguities: This column is one step of the specification build-up in Table 5 and omits part of the conditioning set that the paper's key identifying assumption requires (no own HS GPA, no education-by-institution fixed effects or trends); the paper does not present it as its identified estimate.

Polarity of the outcome: 'Dropout' is recorded as higher_is_less because the concept the variable measures is completion of / persistence in higher education, which the paper's title and framing make explicit ('The Importance of Peer Quality for Completion of Higher Education'). A reader who treats 'dropout' itself as the concept would record higher_is_more.

evidence.how: The table prints no p-values; the coefficient carries '**' and the table note reads '*p < 0.1,**p < 0.05,***p < 0.01', so the printed significance marking means p < 0.05.

The paper never names the estimator. It prints a linear additive estimating equation, reports R-squared and standard errors clustered at the education-by-institution level, and the outcome is a 0/1 indicator, so the estimator is OLS (a linear probability model where the outcome is binary).

claims.statement: Among university STEM enrollments in selective education-by-institution units, a one standard deviation increase in peers' average standardized high school GPA does not measurably change the probability of dropping out of the higher education program the student enrolled in.

definition.value: Leave-one-out average of the standardized high school GPA of the student's peer group, where the peer group is all students enrolling in the same education program at the same institution in the same year; high school GPA is standardized within year of high school graduation. For students without an observable own HS GPA the measure is the peer group average of observable values rather than the leave-one-out average.

timing.value: Predetermined: high school GPA is determined before enrollment in higher education; the peer measure is fixed at the year of enrollment in the education-by-institution cell.

definition.value: Indicator that the student eventually drops out of (rather than completes) the higher education program they enrolled in; students are followed over time until dropout or completion is observed.

timing.value: Measured over the full follow-up of the enrollment spell; the paper states no fixed horizon for the baseline dropout measure.

units.value: change in the probability of dropping out (0-1 scale) per one standard deviation increase in peers' average standardized high school GPA

ambiguities: Polarity of the outcome: 'Dropout' is recorded as higher_is_less because the concept the variable measures is completion of / persistence in higher education, which the paper's title and framing make explicit ('The Importance of Peer Quality for Completion of Higher Education'). A reader who treats 'dropout' itself as the concept would record higher_is_more.

evidence.how: The table prints no p-values; the coefficient carries '*' and the table note reads '*p < 0.1,**p < 0.05,***p < 0.01', so the printed significance marking means p < 0.1.

The paper never names the estimator. It prints a linear additive estimating equation, reports R-squared and standard errors clustered at the education-by-institution level, and the outcome is a 0/1 indicator, so the estimator is OLS (a linear probability model where the outcome is binary).

claims.statement: Among university Health enrollments in selective education-by-institution units, a one standard deviation increase in peers' average standardized high school GPA does not measurably change the probability of dropping out of the higher education program the student enrolled in.

definition.value: Leave-one-out average of the standardized high school GPA of the student's peer group, where the peer group is all students enrolling in the same education program at the same institution in the same year; high school GPA is standardized within year of high school graduation. definition.value: Indicator that the student eventually drops out of (rather than completes) the higher education program they enrolled in; students are followed over time until dropout or completion is observed.

timing.value: Measured over the full follow-up of the enrollment spell; the paper states no fixed horizon for the baseline dropout measure.

units.value: change in the probability of dropping out (0-1 scale) per one standard deviation increase in peers' average standardized high school GPA

key_assumptions.assumption: No education-by-institution specific unobserved time-varying factor drives both the peer composition and the dropout decision beyond what the included education-by-institution linear time trends absorb; the authors concede they cannot rule out systematic correlation with unobservables, in particular in the college sample.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Inclusion of education-by-institution linear time trends; falsification tests in which the spillover effects of adjacent cohorts' ability diminish as the cohort gap expands (Appendix Table A9); Altonji, Elder and Taber (2005) argument that selection on observables indicates selection on unobservables

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on peer-group characteristics: peer groups of three students or fewer, enrollments without an observable peer group ability value, enrollments with only one observable high school GPA in the peer group, and education-by-institution combinations existing for a single cohort are excluded.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The exclusions and their sizes are listed in Section 4.3

implies_edges.from: Sample inclusion: peer group of at least four students with observable peer ability

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across cohorts: the relevant peer group for a student is the own education-by-institution entry cohort, so the ability of adjacent cohorts does not affect own dropout. The paper's own falsification test rejects this for the nearest cohorts -- the ability of peers does have spillover effects on adjacent cohorts -- but finds the effects diminishing as the cohort gap widens.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix Table A9: significant coefficients on the ability of cohorts t-1, t+1 and t+2 whose size and significance diminish as the gap increases

implies_edges.from: Average HS GPA of adjacent (lead and lag) cohorts in the same education-by-institution

key_assumptions.assumption: The peer group is correctly delimited by the education-by-institution entry cohort (split by September/February intake where relevant); the authors acknowledge that in the largest cohorts (up to 1,924 students) not all members are influential peers and that smaller study groups or classrooms are unobserved.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussion in Section 4.1 and robustness to excluding cohorts and programs with more than 500 or 300 students (Table 15)

key_assumptions.assumption: The reduced-form coefficient is not decomposed: it may reflect both contextual peer effects (the effect of peer characteristics) and endogenous peer effects (the effect of peer behaviour) in the sense of Manski (1993), and the paper makes no attempt to separate them.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 5; separation would require additional assumptions and exogenous variation in both contextual and endogenous peer characteristics (Bramoulle, Djebbari and Fortin, 2009)

ambiguities: Polarity of the outcome: 'Dropout' is recorded as higher_is_less because the concept the variable measures is completion of / persistence in higher education, which the paper's title and framing make explicit ('The Importance of Peer Quality for Completion of Higher Education'). A reader who treats 'dropout' itself as the concept would record higher_is_more.

Tables 10 and 11 print no number of observations for any column, so sample_n is left null; the underlying samples are the university and college estimation samples of Tables 6 and 7 (696,602 and 487,488 enrollments) and their gender sub-samples.

In this gender-interacted specification men are the reference group, so the reported coefficient on peers' HS GPA is the peer effect for male students and the interaction term carries the female difference.

evidence.how: The table prints no p-values; the coefficient carries '***' and the table note reads '*p < 0.1,**p < 0.05,***p < 0.01', so the printed significance marking means p < 0.01.

The paper never names the estimator. It prints a linear additive estimating equation, reports R-squared and standard errors clustered at the education-by-institution level, and the outcome is a 0/1 indicator, so the estimator is OLS (a linear probability model where the outcome is binary).
Equation (1) transcribed from the printed equation on page 6; subscripts and Greek letters are rendered in ASCII because the published typesetting is lost in the PDF text layer.

claims.statement: Among all university enrollments in Denmark 1985-2010 in the estimation sample, the effect of peers' high school GPA on the probability of dropping out of the higher education program the student enrolled in does not differ significantly between female and male students.

definition.value: Interaction between an indicator for the student being female and peers' HS GPA (the leave-one-out average of peers' standardized high school GPA); the coefficient is the difference in the peer effect for female relative to male students.

timing.value: Predetermined: high school GPA is determined before enrollment in higher education; the peer measure is fixed at the year of enrollment in the education-by-institution cell.

definition.value: Indicator that the student eventually drops out of (rather than completes) the higher education program they enrolled in; students are followed over time until dropout or completion is observed.

timing.value: Measured over the full follow-up of the enrollment spell; the paper states no fixed horizon for the baseline dropout measure.

units.value: change in the probability of dropping out (0-1 scale) per one standard deviation increase in peers' average standardized high school GPA

The paper's own falsification test rejects this for the nearest cohorts -- the ability of peers does have spillover effects on adjacent cohorts -- but finds the effects diminishing as the cohort gap widens.

key_assumptions.assumption: Reflection bias is avoided because the measure of peer ability is predetermined: high school grades are determined before enrollment in higher education, so the student's own dropout decision and peers' behaviour in higher education cannot feed back into the measured peer ability.

key_assumptions.assumption: No education-by-institution specific unobserved time-varying factor drives both the peer composition and the dropout decision beyond what the included education-by-institution linear time trends absorb; the authors concede they cannot rule out systematic correlation with unobservables, in particular in the college sample.

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across cohorts: the relevant peer group for a student is the own education-by-institution entry cohort, so the ability of adjacent cohorts does not affect own dropout. implies_edges.from: Average HS GPA of adjacent (lead and lag) cohorts in the same education-by-institution

ambiguities: Polarity of the outcome: 'Dropout' is recorded as higher_is_less because the concept the variable measures is completion of / persistence in higher education, which the paper's title and framing make explicit ('The Importance of Peer Quality for Completion of Higher Education'). A reader who treats 'dropout' itself as the concept would record higher_is_more.

Tables 10 and 11 print no number of observations for any column, so sample_n is left null; the underlying samples are the university and college estimation samples of Tables 6 and 7 (696,602 and 487,488 enrollments) and their gender sub-samples.

evidence.how: The table prints no p-values; the coefficient carries '***' and the table note reads '*p < 0.1,**p < 0.05,***p < 0.01', so the printed significance marking means p < 0.01.

The paper never names the estimator. It prints a linear additive estimating equation, reports R-squared and standard errors clustered at the education-by-institution level, and the outcome is a 0/1 indicator, so the estimator is OLS (a linear probability model where the outcome is binary).

definition.value: Leave-one-out average of the standardized high school GPA of the student's peer group, where the peer group is all students enrolling in the same education program at the same institution in the same year; high school GPA is standardized within year of high school graduation. definition.value: Indicator that the student eventually drops out of (rather than completes) the higher education program they enrolled in; students are followed over time until dropout or completion is observed.

timing.value: Measured over the full follow-up of the enrollment spell; the paper states no fixed horizon for the baseline dropout measure.

evidence.how: The table prints no p-values; the coefficient carries '**' and the table note reads '*p < 0.1,**p < 0.05,***p < 0.01', so the printed significance marking means p < 0.05.

claims.statement: Among university enrollments whose own high school GPA is above the 80th percentile of their high school graduation cohort (high-ability students), a larger share of low-GPA peers does not measurably change the probability of dropping out of the higher education program the student enrolled in.

treatment.label: High GPA x Fraction of low-GPA peers

definition.value: Interaction between an indicator that the student's own high school GPA places them in the high ability group (low = below the 20th percentile, high = above the 80th percentile, middle = in between, of the student's high school graduation cohort) and the share of peers whose own high school GPA is below the 20th percentile of their high school graduation cohort, omitting own value. The share of middle-GPA peers is the base category.

timing.value: Predetermined: high school GPA is determined before enrollment in higher education; the peer measure is fixed at the year of enrollment in the education-by-institution cell.

definition.value: Indicator that the student eventually drops out of (rather than completes) the higher education program they enrolled in; students are followed over time until dropout or completion is observed.

timing.value: Measured over the full follow-up of the enrollment spell; the paper states no fixed horizon for the baseline dropout measure.

units.value: change in the probability of dropping out (0-1 scale) per unit increase in the share of peers in the relevant ability group (a 0.10 increase in the share moves dropout by one tenth of the coefficient)

key_assumptions.assumption: The reduced-form coefficient is not decomposed: it may reflect both contextual peer effects (the effect of peer characteristics) and endogenous peer effects (the effect of peer behaviour) in the sense of Manski (1993), and the paper makes no attempt to separate them.

anchor_quote.text: Point estimates suggest that low-ability students reduce their risk of dropout by 1.19 percentage points when the share of high-ability peers increases by 10 percentage points. …

claims.statement: Among university enrollments whose own high school GPA is between the 20th and 80th percentile of their high school graduation cohort (middle-ability students), a larger share of low-GPA peers increases the probability of dropping out of the higher education program the student enrolled in.

treatment.label: Middle GPA x Fraction of low-GPA peers

definition.value: Interaction between an indicator that the student's own high school GPA places them in the middle ability group (low = below the 20th percentile, high = above the 80th percentile, middle = in between, of the student's high school graduation cohort) and the share of peers whose own high school GPA is below the 20th percentile of their high school graduation cohort, omitting own value. The share of middle-GPA peers is the base category.

timing.value: Predetermined: high school GPA is determined before enrollment in higher education; the peer measure is fixed at the year of enrollment in the education-by-institution cell.

definition.value: Indicator that the student eventually drops out of (rather than completes) the higher education program they enrolled in; students are followed over time until dropout or completion is observed.

timing.value: Measured over the full follow-up of the enrollment spell; the paper states no fixed horizon for the baseline dropout measure.

units.value: change in the probability of dropping out (0-1 scale) per unit increase in the share of peers in the relevant ability group (a 0.10 increase in the share moves dropout by one tenth of the coefficient)

implies_edges.from: Sample inclusion: peer group of at least four students with observable peer ability

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across cohorts: the relevant peer group for a student is the own education-by-institution entry cohort, so the ability of adjacent cohorts does not affect own dropout. The paper's own falsification test rejects this for the nearest cohorts -- the ability of peers does have spillover effects on adjacent cohorts -- but finds the effects diminishing as the cohort gap widens.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix Table A9: significant coefficients on the ability of cohorts t-1, t+1 and t+2 whose size and significance diminish as the gap increases

implies_edges.from: Average HS GPA of adjacent (lead and lag) cohorts in the same education-by-institution

key_assumptions.assumption: The peer group is correctly delimited by the education-by-institution entry cohort (split by September/February intake where relevant); the authors acknowledge that in the largest cohorts (up to 1,924 students) not all members are influential peers and that smaller study groups or classrooms are unobserved.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussion in Section 4.1 and robustness to excluding cohorts and programs with more than 500 or 300 students (Table 15)

key_assumptions.assumption: The reduced-form coefficient is not decomposed: it may reflect both contextual peer effects (the effect of peer characteristics) and endogenous peer effects (the effect of peer behaviour) in the sense of Manski (1993), and the paper makes no attempt to separate them.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 5; separation would require additional assumptions and exogenous variation in both contextual and endogenous peer characteristics (Bramoulle, Djebbari and Fortin, 2009)

claims.statement: Among university Social Science enrollments whose own high school GPA is above the 80th percentile of their high school graduation cohort, a larger share of low-GPA peers reduces the probability of dropping out of the higher education program the student enrolled in.

treatment.label: High GPA x Fraction of low-GPA peers

definition.value: Interaction between an indicator that the student's own high school GPA places them in the high ability group (low = below the 20th percentile, high = above the 80th percentile, middle = in between, of the student's high school graduation cohort) and the share of peers whose own high school GPA is below the 20th percentile of their high school graduation cohort, omitting own value. The share of middle-GPA peers is the base category.

timing.value: Predetermined: high school GPA is determined before enrollment in higher education; the peer measure is fixed at the year of enrollment in the education-by-institution cell.

definition.value: Indicator that the student eventually drops out of (rather than completes) the higher education program they enrolled in; students are followed over time until dropout or completion is observed.

timing.value: Measured over the full follow-up of the enrollment spell; the paper states no fixed horizon for the baseline dropout measure.

units.value: change in the probability of dropping out (0-1 scale) per unit increase in the share of peers in the relevant ability group (a 0.10 increase in the share moves dropout by one tenth of the coefficient)

key_assumptions.assumption: The reduced-form coefficient is not decomposed: it may reflect both contextual peer effects (the effect of peer characteristics) and endogenous peer effects (the effect of peer behaviour) in the sense of Manski (1993), and the paper makes no attempt to separate them.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 5; separation would require additional assumptions and exogenous variation in both contextual and endogenous peer characteristics (Bramoulle, Djebbari and Fortin, 2009)

ambiguities: Polarity of the outcome: 'Dropout' is recorded as higher_is_less because the concept the variable measures is completion of / persistence in higher education, which the paper's title and framing make explicit ('The Importance of Peer Quality for Completion of Higher Education'). evidence.how: The table prints no p-values; the coefficient carries '***' and the table note reads '*p < 0.1,**p < 0.05,***p < 0.01', so the printed significance marking means p < 0.01.

The paper never names the estimator. It prints a linear additive estimating equation, reports R-squared and standard errors clustered at the education-by-institution level, and the outcome is a 0/1 indicator, so the estimator is OLS (a linear probability model where the outcome is binary).

ambiguities: Polarity of the outcome: 'Dropout' is recorded as higher_is_less because the concept the variable measures is completion of / persistence in higher education, which the paper's title and framing make explicit ('The Importance of Peer Quality for Completion of Higher Education'). A reader who treats 'dropout' itself as the concept would record higher_is_more.

evidence.how: The table prints no p-values; the coefficient carries '***' and the table note reads '*p < 0.1,**p < 0.05,***p < 0.01', so the printed significance marking means p < 0.01.

The paper never names the estimator. It prints a linear additive estimating equation, reports R-squared and standard errors clustered at the education-by-institution level, and the outcome is a 0/1 indicator, so the estimator is OLS (a linear probability model where the outcome is binary).

key_assumptions.assumption: Reflection bias is avoided because the measure of peer ability is predetermined: high school grades are determined before enrollment in higher education, so the student's own dropout decision and peers' behaviour in higher education cannot feed back into the measured peer ability.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Use of high school GPA, fixed before enrollment, following Lavy, Silva and Weinhardt (2012)

key_assumptions.assumption: No education-by-institution specific unobserved time-varying factor drives both the peer composition and the dropout decision beyond what the included education-by-institution linear time trends absorb; the authors concede they cannot rule out systematic correlation with unobservables, in particular in the college sample.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Inclusion of education-by-institution linear time trends; falsification tests in which the spillover effects of adjacent cohorts' ability diminish as the cohort gap expands (Appendix Table A9); Altonji, Elder and Taber (2005) argument that selection on observables indicates selection on unobservables

key_assumptions.assumption: The estimation sample is conditioned on peer-group characteristics: peer groups of three students or fewer, enrollments without an observable peer group ability value, enrollments with only one observable high school GPA in the peer group, and education-by-institution combinations existing for a single cohort are excluded.
key_assumptions.supported_by: The exclusions and their sizes are listed in Section 4.3

implies_edges.from: Sample inclusion: peer group of at least four students with observable peer ability

key_assumptions.assumption: No interference across cohorts: the relevant peer group for a student is the own education-by-institution entry cohort, so the ability of adjacent cohorts does not affect own dropout. The paper's own falsification test rejects this for the nearest cohorts -- the ability of peers does have spillover effects on adjacent cohorts -- but finds the effects diminishing as the cohort gap widens.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Appendix Table A9: significant coefficients on the ability of cohorts t-1, t+1 and t+2 whose size and significance diminish as the gap increases

implies_edges.from: Average HS GPA of adjacent (lead and lag) cohorts in the same education-by-institution

key_assumptions.assumption: The peer group is correctly delimited by the education-by-institution entry cohort (split by September/February intake where relevant); the authors acknowledge that in the largest cohorts (up to 1,924 students) not all members are influential peers and that smaller study groups or classrooms are unobserved.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Discussion in Section 4.1 and robustness to excluding cohorts and programs with more than 500 or 300 students (Table 15)

key_assumptions.assumption: The reduced-form coefficient is not decomposed: it may reflect both contextual peer effects (the effect of peer characteristics) and endogenous peer effects (the effect of peer behaviour) in the sense of Manski (1993), and the paper makes no attempt to separate them.
key_assumptions.supported_by: Stated in Section 5; separation would require additional assumptions and exogenous variation in both contextual and endogenous peer characteristics (Bramoulle, Djebbari and Fortin, 2009)

robustness_checks: Specification build-up from year FE only to education-by-institution FE plus education-by-institution linear time trends (Table 5, columns 1-5)
Balancing tests of the peer ability measure on student and cohort characteristics (Table 4)
Within-between decomposition of the variance in cohort-level mean HS GPA, raw, net of fixed effects, and net of fixed effects and trends (Table 3)
Restriction to first-time enrollments (Appendix Table A2)
Excluding education-by-institution cells with cohorts larger than 500 or 300 students, and programs whose maximum cohort exceeds 500 or 300 (Table 15)
Dropping education-by-institution specific linear time trends (Appendix Table A8)
Falsification tests regressing dropout on the average ability of cohorts t-5 to t+5 (Appendix Table A9)
Relative (within education-by-institution) rather than absolute ability ranking (Table 14, Appendix Table A7)

unresolved_confounders: Systematic correlations between the within education-by-institution variation in peer ability and unobservables behind the balancing-test correlations in the college sample: 'We cannot rule out this possibility even though we include all of the balancing variables as controls in our estimation model.' (p. 7)
Separation of contextual from endogenous peer effects: 'Our analysis will document the existence of peer effects without making further attempt to separate the effects.' (p. 6)

ambiguities: Polarity of the outcome: 'Dropout' is recorded as higher_is_less because the concept the variable measures is completion of / persistence in higher education, which the paper's title and framing make explicit ('The Importance of Peer Quality for Completion of Higher Education'). A reader who treats 'dropout' itself as the concept would record higher_is_more.

evidence.how: The table prints no p-values; the coefficient carries '***' and the table note reads '*p < 0.1,**p < 0.05,***p < 0.01', so the printed significance marking means p < 0.01.

The paper never names the estimator. It prints a linear additive estimating equation, reports R-squared and standard errors clustered at the education-by-institution level, and the outcome is a 0/1 indicator, so the estimator is OLS (a linear probability model where the outcome is binary).
Equation (1) transcribed from the printed equation on page 6; subscripts and Greek letters are rendered in ASCII because the published typesetting is lost in the PDF text layer.
